sections.h2: Does New Mexico charge an estate tax?
sections.html:
In practice, no. The state's estate tax was phased out because of federal tax law changes as of January 1, 2005. The Estate Tax Act, Section 7-7-1 NMSA 1978 and following, is still on the books, and the Taxation and Revenue Department still asks for paperwork in one situation.

If the estate has to file the federal estate tax return, Form 706, for any reason, the personal representative also files a New Mexico return, form RPD-41058. When the department receives both, it issues a certificate of no tax due for the estate's records. The state due date is the federal due date, including any extension of time for the federal return.

The state tax equals the federal credit on the net estate. Returns and payments go to the New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department, P.O. Box 25123, Santa Fe, NM 87504-5123. For help, call (505) 827-0763 or email Other.Taxes@tax.nm.gov.

New Mexico does not impose an inheritance tax. Heirs who receive a house, cash or other property do not owe the state a tax for receiving it. With no estate tax in practice and no inheritance tax, the state itself takes nothing from the transfer.

sections.h2: When the federal estate tax applies
sections.html:
Only large estates owe federal estate tax. For a death in 2026 the basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000, equal to a credit of $5,945,800 at 2026 rates, and most estates sit well under it.

The federal return is due nine months after the date of death. Some families file even with no tax due, to elect portability of a deceased spouse's unused exclusion.

Taxes an heir may meet when selling an inherited New Mexico house
TaxDoes it apply to a New Mexico heir selling a house?
New Mexico estate taxPhased out as of January 1, 2005; a no-tax-due certificate is issued if a Form 706 was required
New Mexico inheritance taxNone
Federal estate taxOnly for estates above the exclusion, $15,000,000 for 2026 deaths
Income tax on estate earningsYes, if the estate or trust earns income; filed on form FID-1

sections.h2: Income tax on what the estate earns
sections.html:
An estate pays income tax on what it earns while it is open, at personal income tax rates. The state's fiduciary income tax return is form FID-1. This is a different tax from the estate tax, because it is based on income the estate or trust generates rather than on the value of what the decedent left.

A house sale during administration can generate gain. Keep the settlement statement, the date-of-death value and a record of repair and carrying costs, because the estate's accountant will need them.

sections.h2: Tax on gain when an heir sells
sections.html:
Usually little, since inherited property generally gets a fresh basis equal to its fair market value on the date of death. That holds whether or not an estate tax return was filed. A sale near that value leaves little or no gain to report.

An estate that must file Form 706 has to keep its basis consistent with the value finally reported for estate tax. With no such statement in hand, the basis can be the appraised value at death used for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes.

  • Order a date-of-death appraisal early, before repairs or cleanup change the condition.
  • Gather the death certificate, the court's letters, and the deed or tax record that shows how title was held.
  • Tell the accountant if you or your spouse gave the property to the decedent within one year before death, because a different basis rule applies then.

sections.h2: Probate and selling an inherited house
sections.html:
In most cases a house must pass through probate first. Real estate titled in the decedent's name needs it. Real estate held as joint tenants, or with a recorded transfer on death deed, does not.

The small-estate affidavit rarely helps, because a small estate means under $50,000 with no real property in it. One narrow route exists for a surviving spouse. The primary residence can pass by affidavit under Section 45-3-1205 when at least six months have gone by, no probate has been filed, and the assessed value does not exceed $500,000, among other conditions. The affidavit goes to the county clerk where the home sits.

Every other case is filed in probate court in the county where the decedent lived. The court charges $30 to file, and the filing window runs from 5 days to 3 years after death. A personal representative's deed may be needed to move title. Even after three years, a probate can be opened solely to transfer title to heirs.

sections.h2: Property tax during and after probate
sections.html:
The tax bill does not pause while probate runs, and it can jump afterward. Real property tax is a first lien from January 1 of the tax year, ranking ahead of other interests. No filing is needed to create it, so an old unpaid bill is still there after the owner dies.

Residential value can rise only 3 percent a year, until ownership changes and the cap resets. Several transfers escape that reset: to a surviving spouse, to a child who lives in the home as a principal residence, and to or from certain revocable trusts. An heir who lives there but stops qualifying for the head of household exemption is treated as a new owner starting the first tax year afterward.

Selling to an outside buyer is a change of ownership, so the value resets for the buyer. Taxes are due November 10 and April 10, with interest after December 10 and May 10.

Start with who can legally sign, then check where the taxes stand. Work through these in order:

  • Obtain letters from the probate court, or confirm a recorded transfer on death deed or joint tenancy.
  • Ask the county treasurer for the balance owed, including any earlier-year bill left unpaid.
  • Have the accountant decide whether a Form 706 or a state RPD-41058 is needed.
  • Record any deed with the county clerk, because an unrecorded deed does not affect title against a later purchaser.

Call the clerk and treasurer in the county where the house sits. Once authority and taxes are settled, the title company can set a closing date and pay any tax balance from the proceeds. Heirs who live elsewhere often prefer a cash sale, since it skips the buyer's loan approval, repairs and repeated showings.

faqs.q: Does New Mexico have an estate tax in 2026?
faqs.a: Effectively no. The state estate tax was phased out as of January 1, 2005. If a federal Form 706 is required, the estate also files form RPD-41058 and receives a certificate of no tax due.

faqs.q: Does New Mexico have an inheritance tax?
faqs.a: No. New Mexico does not impose an inheritance tax, so heirs owe the state nothing for receiving a house or cash.

faqs.q: What is the federal estate tax exemption for 2026?
faqs.a: The basic exclusion amount for 2026 deaths is $15,000,000. The return is due nine months after the date of death.

faqs.q: Do I need probate to sell an inherited house?
faqs.a: Usually, unless the house passed by joint tenancy or a recorded transfer on death deed. The small-estate affidavit does not cover real property, with a narrow spousal exception for a primary residence of $500,000 or less.

faqs.q: What is my tax basis in an inherited house?
faqs.a: Generally the fair market value on the date of death. A date-of-death appraisal is the usual proof.
